name: Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga)
place: Zoétélé, village of the Mvog Mezanga (Dja-et-Lobo, South)
overview: In the majority in their locality of Zoétélé, the Foŋ live alongside the Esə, Ŋdoŋ and Jəmdək, all Bulu. Like the other Beti, they say they came from the other bank of the Sanaga. Organised around kinship and inherited specialisms (dancers, hunters, carpenters), they live from cocoa, timber and cassava sticks, and dance the eɲəŋgə to the sound of the mvet.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, neighbouring the Esə, Ŋdoŋ and Jəmdək, all Bulu.
The foŋ speech variety is found in Ebolowa, Ngoazip and Biwong-Bane.
The great foŋ families marry among themselves and with their neighbours, provided they are not from the same family.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land; like all the Beti, the Foŋ tell of the crossing of the Sanaga.
Notable places in Zoétélé: the Akɔɔ river and the Ŋkɔ Oboŋ forest.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Kinship organises society; decisions are made by consensus at the grouping's chiefdom.
Friendly relations, with strict respect for elders and the hierarchy (chief, patriarch, notables).
Specialities, sometimes hereditary: dancers and instrumentalists, hunters and farmers, tree fellers and carpenters.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband.
The boy becomes a man by marrying, clearing his plantation and building his house; the young woman, through marriage and motherhood.
Formerly, a wife was sometimes reserved from the cradle, then came the bride price; today, everyone chooses.
Bride price: palm wine (ako) and animals (goats, sometimes tortoises).

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: The old cults were abandoned with the arrival of Western religions, and divination is practised discreetly.
It used to be possible to get in touch with the dead to converse or to solve a problem of the group.
Taboos: incest, any relationship with one's father's wife.
Viper is eaten only if you have killed one yourself, or if your father gives it to you.
Incest required an expiatory rite (evatso); quarantine (miŋbok mi ŋnam) forbade appearing in public.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Sale of wood, cocoa, farming, sale of cassava sticks.
The land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought or received as a gift.
Crafts: carrying baskets (miŋkwe), baskets (bijat, miŋkun), shelves (məkaŋ, etaŋ).

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Old clothing: obom, saŋda, bibwi, loincloth of leaves (məŋja).
People still turn to traditional medicine, for what modern medicine does not cure.
Beauty: being well dressed, tattoos (otwi), hairstyle, scarification and nose piercing for men; clothing and braids for women.
Courtship: gifts to the young girl; culinary talent.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: eɲəŋgə, aɲəŋzɔk, olaŋtsa, məŋgan; instruments: balafons (məŋdzaŋ), mvet (mvɛt ojəŋ), tam-tams (miŋku), drums (məŋgɔm).
Dances: ozila, eɲəŋgə, aɲəŋ, olaŋtsa, məŋgan.
No community festival of its own.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: According to tradition, the ancestor Oyono Eyamo, born a girl, was turned into a boy by a rite performed in the bed of the river Akɔ.

sections.title: The names
items: No particular structure; the name depends on circumstances and does not change.
The real name and the pseudonym (dzoe məbadan), the appellative à- and the sung name (ŋdan) are used.
The founding ancestor, Oyono Eyamo, is “the standing elephant” (zɔa etələ).

lessons.title: Who are the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, neighbouring the Esə, Ŋdoŋ and Jəmdək, all Bulu. • The Foŋ speech variety is found at Ebolowa, Ngoazip and Biwong-Bane. • The large Foŋ families marry among themselves and with their neighbours, provided they are not of the same family. • Ancestral land; like all the Beti, the Foŋ tell of the crossing of the Sanaga. • Notable places at Zoétélé: the Akɔɔ river and the Ŋkɔ Oboŋ forest.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their locality of Zoétélé, the Foŋ live alongside the Esə, Ŋdoŋ and Jəmdək, all Bulu. Like the other Beti, they say they came from the other bank of the Sanaga. Organised around kinship and inherited specialisms (dancers, hunters, carpenters), they live from cocoa, timber and cassava sticks, and dance the eɲəŋgə to the sound of the mvet.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Kinship organises society; decisions are taken by consensus at the chiefdom of the groupement. • Convivial relations, in strict respect of elders and hierarchy (chief, patriarch, notables). • Specialisations, sometimes hereditary: dancers and instrumentalists, hunters and farmers, tree fellers and carpenters.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Kinship organises society; decisions are taken by consensus at the grouping's chiefdom. Relations are convivial, with strict respect for elders and for the hierarchy (chief, patriarch, notables). Specialisms, sometimes hereditary: dancers and instrumentalists, hunters and farmers, tree fellers and carpenters.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: kpəm without salt (pəm məŋdim), groundnut dishes (ŋnam owoŋdo), məŋdip zɔŋ, esɔŋ. • Drinks: palm wine (mejɔa malen). • Sale of timber, cocoa, farming, sale of cassava sticks.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) mainly eat unsalted kpəm, ŋnam owoŋdo, məŋdip zɔŋ, esɔŋ. Traditional drinks: mejɔa malen. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

steps.instruction: Among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), traditional dances (eɲəŋgə, ozila, olaŋtsa) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: məŋdzaŋ, mvet, miŋku, məŋgɔm.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Sale of timber, cocoa, farming, sale of cassava sticks. • Land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought or received as a gift. • Crafts: baskets (miŋkwe), baskets (bijat, miŋkun), shelves (məkaŋ, etaŋ).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Sale of timber, cocoa, farming, sale of cassava sticks. The land belongs to the members of the group; it is bought or received as a gift.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: sauf si on l'a tuée ou si le père la donne

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The old cults were abandoned with the arrival of Western religions, and divination is practised discreetly. • It was possible to make contact with the dead to converse or to resolve a problem of the group. • Taboos: incest, any relationship with one's father's wife. • Viper is eaten only if one has killed one, or if one's father gives it. • Incest required an expiatory rite (evatso); quarantine (miŋbok mi ŋnam) forbade appearing in public.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The old cults were abandoned with the arrival of Western religions, and divination is practised discreetly. People could make contact with the dead to converse or to resolve a problem of the group.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: The old cults were abandoned with the arrival of Western religions, and divination is practised discreetly. People could make contact with the dead to converse or to resolve a problem of the group.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Foŋ
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Foŋ. • Greeting formulas: Mbolo = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Mbəmba tse = morning greeting (one person); Ma suk mina = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Fɔg, Bae, La, ɲin, Tan. • The founding ancestor, Oyono Eyamo, is “the standing elephant” (zɔa etələ). • According to tradition, the ancestor Oyono Eyamo, born a girl, was turned into a boy by a rite performed in the bed of the Akɔ river.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Foŋ are the first steps towards communicating with the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Foŋ.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Foŋ are the first steps towards communicating with the Foŋ (Mvog Mezanga). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
